clinicalPearls: Immune destruction of red cells by autoantibodies, usually IgG, that bind optimally at body temperature
The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive, typically for IgG with or without complement
The blood film shows spherocytes and features of haemolysis with reticulocytosis, raised lactate dehydrogenase, raised unconjugated bilirubin and low haptoglobin
It may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to lymphoproliferative disease, autoimmune disorders such as lupus, or drugs
Extravascular haemolysis predominates, with red cells removed in the spleen
Corticosteroids are first-line, with rituximab, splenectomy and other immunosuppression for refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: In warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, IgG autoantibodies bind red cell surface antigens at 37 degrees Celsius. Antibody-coated cells are recognised by splenic macrophages through Fc receptors and are partially or wholly phagocytosed, producing spherocytes and predominantly extravascular haemolysis. The bone marrow compensates with brisk reticulocytosis. Secondary forms arise when an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder, or a drug, disturbs immune tolerance and drives autoantibody production.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocytes and blood film for spherocytes
Investigation for secondary causes (lymphoproliferative, autoimmune, drugs)
Assessment for coexisting immune thrombocytopenia (Evans syndrome)
redFlags: Rapidly falling haemoglobin with cardiovascular compromise
Evidence of an underlying lymphoma or lupus
Severe haemolysis unresponsive to first-line therapy
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond to corticosteroids, but relapse is common and refractory disease requires escalation; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying disorder.
pitfalls: Not investigating for a secondary cause, especially lymphoma
Transfusion difficulties from pan-reactive autoantibodies masking alloantibodies
Attributing spherocytes solely to hereditary spherocytosis
management: Induce remission with corticosteroids such as prednisolone as first-line therapy
For refractory or relapsing disease, add rituximab and consider splenectomy or immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, ciclosporin or mycophenolate mofetil
Give folic acid supplementation to support the compensatory reticulocytosis
Identify and treat any secondary cause by withdrawing an implicated drug or managing underlying lymphoproliferative or connective tissue disease such as lupus
Transfuse the best-matched, warmed red cells only for symptomatic or life-threatening anaemia, alerting the laboratory to autoantibody-related crossmatch difficulty
Provide venous thromboembolism prophylaxis during active haemolysis
Monitor haemolysis markers and the full blood count, and screen for coexisting immune thrombocytopenia (Evans syndrome)
Refer to haematology and escalate urgently for haemodynamic compromise or a fulminant haemolytic crisis
